analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal law requiring prevailing local wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have ended prevailing-wage requirements on federal construction work, was introduced in May 1999 with 7 Republican sponsors and never received a committee hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1931, the Davis-Bacon Act has required contractors on federally financed construction projects to pay workers the locally prevailing wage, and the Copeland Act requires the Labor Department to enforce related reporting rules for those contractors. This bill would have repealed both laws. Supporters argued this would cut taxpayer costs on federal projects; workers on those projects would no longer be guaranteed prevailing pay.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be contractors and subcontractors on federally funded construction, whose labor costs would fall because they could pay market or lower wages instead of the locally prevailing rate. Taxpayers could see some savings on federal construction bids if lower wages translated into lower bids, though research cited in policy debates is mixed on whether overall project costs actually fall.

how_it_helps.text: Repealing Davis-Bacon removes the requirement to pay the locally prevailing wage to laborers and mechanics on federally financed or assisted construction, alteration, and repair of public buildings and public works [S2].
Repealing the Copeland Act removes the Labor Department's authority to regulate contractors and subcontractors on those projects, eliminating associated compliance and reporting rules [S2].
The repeal would take effect 30 days after enactment but would not disturb contracts already in existence or bids already outstanding [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects, particularly laborers and mechanics who rely on the prevailing-wage floor, would likely earn less; the repeal would also remove federal rules that many in the construction trades see as protecting local wage standards and limiting undercutting by out-of-area low-wage contractors.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate the only federal prevailing-wage floor, exposing federally funded construction workers to lower pay and weakening local wage standards in the construction industry [S2].

Removing the Copeland Act would strip the Labor Department's regulatory oversight of contractors and subcontractors on public works, reducing enforcement of payroll and reporting rules on those jobs [S2].

Supporters of repeal argue prevailing-wage rules raise federal construction costs; this bill offered no replacement mechanism, so any projected taxpayer savings would come directly out of wages on federally funded jobs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's promised benefit was lower federal construction costs through cheaper labor. The cost fell entirely on construction workers, who would lose the prevailing-wage floor that has applied to federally funded projects since 1931. There is no offsetting protection in the bill for affected workers, so the tradeoff is essentially a transfer from federal-project workers to contractors, with uncertain savings to taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 1999, referred to the Senate committee that handles labor matters, and sat there until Congress ended in January 2001 without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Smith of New Hampshire introduced the bill on May 27, 1999, joined by five other Republican senators: Inhofe, Thurmond, Nickles, Helms, and Cochran [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S1].
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects kept the prevailing-wage and enforcement rules the bill would have repealed, since the bill died without action; contractors never obtained the lower labor costs it would have allowed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal construction workers kept wage protections

for.name: Sen. Bob Smith
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Hampshire; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon and Copeland Acts and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Inhofe, Thurmond, Nickles, Helms, and Cochran
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill an all-Republican, 7-sponsor start.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 27, 1999 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and the all-Republican referral to the labor committee was followed by no action.

industries.note: Repeal would let them pay market rather than prevailing wages on federally funded projects, cutting their labor costs. The gain comes directly out of construction workers' pay, so the industry's interest in this bill ran against the workers it employs.

The prevailing-wage floor and Copeland Act reporting rules are the main protections for pay standards on federal projects; repealing both would leave these workers with less pay and less oversight of contractor payroll practices. Their interest ran alongside ordinary taxpayers' interest in fair local wage standards.
